unit.title: Participate in online networks and social media

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Describe three different kinds of online network or social media, and say how each could be used in a workplace such as a fabrication shop or a villa.
essays.modelAnswer: A social networking site lets people make a profile, post photos and messages, and follow others. A fabrication shop can use a business page to show photos of finished gates and grills, and a villa can share pictures of its rooms and view to attract guests. A messaging app with group chats lets a team send quick messages. A supervisor can send the day's job list to welders on site, or the housekeeping team can share which rooms are ready. A professional networking site is used to show work history, skills and certificates. Workers can use it to find jobs and link with employers, and a business can use it to find staff. Other kinds include video-sharing sites, where a business can post short videos of its work, and forums, where workers ask and answer trade questions. Each must be used in line with the employer's rules.
markingPoints: Social networking site described, with a suitable work use
Messaging app or group chat described, with a suitable work use
Professional networking site described, with a suitable work use
Another kind (video-sharing site, forum) or the point that the employer's rules apply

essays.stem: Explain the steps to set up a safe and professional profile on a social media or professional networking site.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read the site's rules and privacy terms. I sign up with an email address I check often, choose a sensible username, and set a strong password that I use nowhere else. I turn on two-step verification, so a code is sent to my phone when someone logs in from a new device. I add a clear, friendly photo of my face, and write a short, honest description of my trade and skills, such as "Level 2 welding trainee" or "Villa housekeeping attendant". I do not add my home address, date of birth, ID number or bank details. Then I open the privacy settings and choose who can see my posts, my friends list and my contact details, and I turn off location sharing. Finally I view the profile as the public would see it, and fix anything that does not look professional.
markingPoints: Read the terms; sign up with a sensible username and a strong, unique password
Turn on two-step verification
Professional photo and an honest description of trade and skills
Leave out private details such as home address, date of birth, ID and bank details
Set privacy settings, turn off location, and check the public view

essays.stem: Describe five rules of good manners (netiquette) for posting and messaging online at work.
essays.modelAnswer: First, think before you post: ask whether you would be happy for your supervisor, a customer or your family to read it. Second, be polite and respectful, even when you disagree, and never insult, threaten or make fun of anyone. Third, write clearly, with proper words and punctuation in work messages, and do not type in all capitals, because it looks like shouting. Fourth, respect privacy: do not share other people's photos, phone numbers or personal stories without their permission, and do not post about customers or guests. Fifth, keep work groups for work: stay on the topic, do not send chain messages or jokes that may offend, and do not message co-workers late at night unless it is urgent. It is also good manners to check facts before sharing and to answer messages in good time.
markingPoints: Think before posting: would you be happy for your boss or family to see it
Be polite and respectful; no insults, threats or mocking
Write clearly in work messages; no all capitals
Respect privacy: ask before sharing others' photos or details
Keep work groups on topic and message at suitable times

essays.stem: Explain how you would protect your social media accounts from being hacked, and what you would do if one was hacked.
essays.modelAnswer: To protect my accounts I use a long, strong password for each one and never use the same password twice. I turn on two-step verification. I never share my password, even with friends, and I always log out on shared computers. I keep the apps and my phone up to date and download apps only from the official store. I do not click strange links or answer messages asking for codes or passwords. If an account is hacked, I act quickly. I try to log in and change the password at once, then use the security settings to log out all other devices. If I cannot get in, I use the site's account recovery or report steps. I warn my friends and contacts not to trust messages from the account. If it is a work account, I tell my supervisor straight away. Then I check for posts or messages the hacker sent and delete them.
markingPoints: Strong, different password for each account, and two-step verification
Never share passwords; log out on shared devices; keep apps updated
Do not click strange links or give out codes
If hacked: change the password, log out other devices, or use the site's recovery and report steps
Warn contacts, tell the supervisor if it is a work account, and remove the hacker's posts

essays.stem: Explain why a business has a social media policy, and list the kinds of things it usually tells staff.
essays.modelAnswer: A business has a social media policy to protect its good name, its customers and its staff. One careless post can upset a customer, break a guest's privacy, give away business information or start a public argument. The policy makes it clear what staff may and may not do, so everyone follows the same rules. It usually tells staff not to share private business information, such as prices, plans or security details. It says not to post photos or details of customers, guests or their property without permission. It names who is allowed to speak for the business on its official pages. It asks staff to be respectful about the employer, co-workers and other businesses, and says that bullying online will be dealt with. It may also say when staff may use their phones at work, and what will happen if the rules are broken.
markingPoints: Reason: protects the business's name, its customers or guests, and its staff
Do not share private business information
Do not post customers, guests or their property without permission
Only named people speak for the business on official pages
Respectful behaviour, phone use at work, and what happens if rules are broken

essays.stem: A fabrication team has just finished a large set of gates at a customer's home in Mandeville, and the team wants to post photos online. Describe how they should do this in a safe and professional way.
essays.modelAnswer: First they should ask the customer whether photos can be posted, and also check with the employer, because the photos show the business's work. They should agree what can be shown. When taking the photos, they should leave out anything that shows where the customer lives, such as the house number, a street sign or a car's licence plate, and they should not show the family or anything valuable. They should switch off location tagging. The photos should be clear, well lit and show neat, finished work, with tools and offcuts cleared away. The post should go on the business's own page, or be shared by the person the employer has chosen, with a short polite caption about the job but no address. After posting, they should reply politely to comments and pass any questions about prices or bookings to the supervisor.
markingPoints: Get permission from the customer and the employer first
Hide the address, licence plates, people and valuables; turn off location
Clear, tidy photos of the finished work
Post on the business page (or by the chosen person) with a suitable caption and no private details
Reply politely to comments and pass enquiries to the supervisor

essays.stem: A guest posts an angry review online saying their villa room was not clean. Describe how the business should answer it online, and why the way it answers matters.
essays.modelAnswer: The person chosen by the business should reply, not any worker who happens to see it. They should answer fairly quickly, within a day if possible, so the guest knows they are being heard. The reply should be calm and polite, and thank the guest for the feedback. It should say sorry that the stay was not what they expected, without arguing or blaming anyone by name. It must not show the guest's booking details, room number or other private information in public. It should say briefly what is being done, such as checking the room with the housekeeping team, and invite the guest to message or call so the matter can be sorted out in private. Then the business must really fix the problem. The answer matters because other people reading the review judge the business by its reply. A calm, helpful answer can win back the guest and show future guests that the business cares.
markingPoints: The chosen person replies, and replies promptly
Calm and polite: thanks the guest and says sorry, with no arguing or blaming
No private guest details in public
Says what is being done, moves the talk to private messages, and fixes the problem
Why: other readers judge the business by the reply; it can win the guest back

essays.stem: Explain how you can check whether a story or message you see online is true before you share it.
essays.modelAnswer: First I stop and do not share it straight away, even if it seems urgent. I look at who posted it. Is it a known news service, a government body or the company itself, or is it an unknown account or a forwarded message with no name? I read the whole story, not just the headline, and check the date, because old stories are often shared again. I look for warning signs, such as a shocking headline in capitals, many spelling mistakes, or a request to share with everyone now. I check whether trusted news sources or the official body, such as the water company or the parish council, are saying the same thing. For a photo, I can do a picture search to see if it is old or from somewhere else. If I still cannot be sure, I do not share it. If it is about work, I ask my supervisor.
markingPoints: Pause and do not share at once
Check who posted it and whether the source is known and trusted
Read the whole story, check the date and look for warning signs
Check with trusted news or the official body (or a picture search)
If still unsure, do not share; ask the supervisor about work matters

essays.stem: Explain why workers should limit personal social media use during working hours. Give examples from a workshop and from a villa.
essays.modelAnswer: Using a phone for personal social media at work takes attention away from the job. In a workshop this can be dangerous. A welder or a grinder operator who looks at a phone can lose focus, and a person who walks while texting may trip over cables or walk into a work area without PPE. Phones should never be used while running a machine or doing hot work. In a villa, a housekeeper who keeps checking a phone may leave a job half done or seem rude to guests, and the guest may feel that the staff do not care. Personal use also wastes paid working time, so jobs take longer and deadlines are missed. There is also a risk of posting something about work, a guest or a customer without thinking. Workers should follow the employer's rules, keep the phone away during tasks, and use it for personal things only on breaks or in an emergency.
markingPoints: It takes attention away from the job and lowers the quality of work
Workshop example: danger near machines, hot work, cables or without PPE
Villa example: jobs left undone or guests feel ignored
Wasted paid time, missed deadlines, or careless posts about work
Follow the employer's rules; use the phone only on breaks or in an emergency

essays.stem: Describe how a small business, such as a welding shop or a villa, can use social media to attract customers, and give two things it must take care with.
essays.modelAnswer: A small business can make an official page with its name, logo, area, opening hours and contact number. It can post clear photos and short videos of its real work, such as finished gates, burglar bars and railings, or clean rooms, the pool and the view at a villa. Posts should be regular, short and in plain words, with a few hashtags so new people can find them. The business can share customer reviews, with permission, and special offers for slow seasons. It should answer messages and comments quickly and politely, because a fast reply often turns into a sale. Two things to take care with are privacy and honesty. The business must get permission before showing customers, guests or their homes, and must not post their details. Its photos and prices must be true and up to date, because false adverts damage trust. It should also not use other people's photos without the right to do so.
markingPoints: An official page with clear contact details
Regular, clear photos or videos of real work, with suitable hashtags
Share reviews or offers and answer messages quickly and politely
Take care with privacy: permission before showing customers, guests or their homes
Take care with honesty and copyright: true photos and prices, no borrowed photos

practical1.title: Plan and prepare professional posts for a small business page
practical1.brief: As a group, plan and prepare three posts for a small business page. Choose one business from the assessor's cards: a fabrication shop or a villa. (1) Together, write a short set of rules for the page on chart paper: what may be posted, what must never be posted, and who answers the public. (2) Take or choose three photos at the Centre, for example a finished practice piece in the workshop or a made-up bed in the training room. Show no one's face unless they agree, no names, and no location. (3) Each member writes at least one caption, in plain polite words, with up to three suitable hashtags. (4) Each member checks another member's post against the group's rules and the assessor's checklist, and marks any change needed. (5) Put the posts on the Centre's practice page, set so that only the assessor's test group can see them, or lay them out on poster paper if there is no practice page. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: Chart paper, markers and sticky notes
A phone or camera for photos
The Centre's practice social media page or account, if available (no personal accounts)
Printed post templates and a post-checking checklist from the assessor
A computer or tablet with internet, if the practice page is used
photos: The group's page rules written on chart paper
The three chosen photos, showing no private details
The draft captions with hashtags, before checking
Members checking each other's posts with the checklist
The finished posts on the practice page screen, or on the poster
The audience or privacy setting chosen for the posts
checklist: Took part in writing the group's page rules
Chose or took a suitable photo with permission and no private details or location
Wrote a clear, polite caption with correct spelling and suitable hashtags
Checked another member's post against the rules and suggested a fair change
Set or explained the right audience or privacy setting for the posts
Explained to the assessor why one post is suitable and one idea was not
Spoke and worked respectfully with the group
safety: Use only the Centre's practice page or account; never use or show a personal password
Ask before photographing anyone, and show no names, addresses or locations
When taking photos in the workshop or a work area, follow that area's rules and PPE, and never use a phone near a running machine or hot work
Tell the assessor at once about any upsetting message or comment

practical2.title: Secure an account and role-play replies to comments, messages and scams
practical2.brief: As a group, show that you can keep an account safe and deal with what comes in. Stage 1: on the Centre's practice account (on a Centre phone or computer), set a strong password, turn on two-step verification, choose who can see posts and contact details, and turn off location sharing. Each member sets or explains at least one setting while the others check. Photograph each screen, with any passwords and personal details hidden. Stage 2: the assessor gives out printed cards: a rude comment, a kind review, a question about prices, a scam message, a false news post and a "friend" asking for a password. Each member takes one card and role-plays it with another member, then writes the reply or the action on the group's response sheet. In a group of 4, one member takes two cards. Stage 3: as a group, make a one-page poster of online safety tips for staff. Photograph each stage and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: A Centre phone or computer with the Centre's practice account
Printed scenario cards from the assessor
A response sheet for the group's written replies
A phone or camera for photos
photos: The password and two-step verification screens, with passwords hidden
The privacy and location settings chosen
A role play in progress, with the scenario card shown
The completed response sheet with each member's reply
checklist: Set or explained a security or privacy setting correctly
Kept passwords and personal details hidden in all photos
Gave a calm, polite and professional reply to their scenario
Spotted the scam or false news card and gave the correct action
Did not share private details of customers, guests or co-workers in replies
Added at least one correct tip to the safety poster
Listened to others and took part fully in the role plays
safety: Use only the Centre's practice account and devices; never use a personal account
Never show a real password or code in a photo
Do not click any real link: the scam examples are printed on cards
Tell the assessor if anything online upsets you
